THE THREAD THROUGH IT ALL

BUILD THE INTUITION

Three things an EKG is really telling you.

01

What does a negative voltage mean?

+

The input marked + is at a lower electric potential than the input marked −. Those symbols name the amplifier’s inputs; they do not force an electrode to be positively or negatively charged.

A volt is a joule per coulomb. Voltage describes an energy difference per unit charge between two places.

02

How can a depolarized heart look flat?

+

If tissue has nearly the same membrane voltage everywhere, there is little spatial contrast to drive an external dipole. In the ideal uniform strand, the two electrodes read the same potential.

This helps explain the near-isoelectric ST segment even though ventricular cells are still depolarized. A flat lead can also result from cancellation or its orientation.

03

Where does the reference zero come from?

+

A lead needs a comparison point, not a universal zero. Lead II subtracts the right-arm potential from the left-leg potential. Chest leads compare their electrode with an average of three limb potentials: the Wilson central terminal.

The right-leg electrode commonly controls body bias and suppresses shared interference. It is not the negative input of every lead.

Designed for understanding · EKG and ECG mean the same thing
UNDER THE ANIMATION

From ions to a measured voltage.

Three related quantities. Three different measurements.
01 · ACROSS A MEMBRANE
Vm = φi − φe

Inside minus immediately outside the cell. Here, a representative ventricular action potential runs from −90 to +25 mV.

02 · AT A BODY LOCATION
φe(r) = Σ Ij / (4πσdj)

Current sources and sinks establish a potential in conductive tissue. This expression assumes an infinite, uniform conductor.

03 · BETWEEN TWO ELECTRODES
Vlead = φ+ − φ−

The amplifier compares two external potentials. It does not add up all the cells’ membrane voltages.

1. A little charge can make a large membrane voltage

The lipid bilayer separates conductive solutions and acts as a capacitor. In the lumped illustration, Qinner = CmVm. Only a small imbalance of ions near the membrane surfaces is needed; the bulk fluid on both sides remains nearly electrically neutral. Different ion concentrations and selective membrane permeability establish electrochemical gradients.

For an illustrative total capacitance of 100 pF, changing from −90 to +25 mV changes the inner-face charge by 11.5 pC, about 7.2 × 10⁷ elementary charges. This is a calculated example, not a universal cell size. Surface signs and particle counts are greatly exaggerated. Sodium and potassium concentration gradients barely change within one beat.

In a working ventricular cell, fast Na⁺ entry produces the upstroke; inward Ca²⁺ and outward K⁺ currents help sustain the plateau; net outward ionic current, largely K⁺, brings the voltage back down. Pumps maintain gradients over time. They do not suddenly “reset” each action potential. [1] [2]

2. Neighboring cells turn a membrane change into a current loop

Current passes through gap junctions into neighboring cells. Return current flows through extracellular fluid. During a traveling depolarization, inward membrane current creates an extracellular sink behind the front, with a balancing source ahead. In the simplified strand, the dipole points from sink toward source. [3]

Jj+½ = −G(Vm,j+1 − Vm,j)
Ij = Jj−½ − Jj+½
Σ Ij = 0

Chapter 2 uses 81 prescribed AP elements with explicit AT + APD timing. Chapter 3 retains a 41-element source-field illustration. Zero current at the strand ends makes every outward source balance an inward sink. Their extracellular potentials are summed through a homogeneous conductor. The parallel rows are a drawing of working ventricular muscle, not an anatomical reconstruction. The default current overlay enlarges arrows to show direction; the numerical current retains its fixed reference. The optional strength view scales the glyphs with current, and exact zero draws no flow. The closed path includes intracellular and extracellular current; it is not a closed electric-field line. A softening distance avoids singularities in the source-field illustration. This is a reduced source model, not a numerical solution of all membrane channels or the bidomain equations.

3. Why polarity changes

A depolarization sequence toward the positive input gives an upward deflection in this simple geometry. Recovery in that same spatial order reverses the voltage gradient. Reversing both the process and its spatial order can produce an upright recovery deflection. Recovery marks cells finishing their own action potentials; it is not a second regenerative excitation traveling backward. [4]

The human T wave integrates recovery differences across multiple cardiac axes. The reversed strand is an experiment about signs, not a claim that every human ventricular cell recovers in exactly the opposite order. Human optical mapping shows why a simple transmural account is incomplete. [6]

4. References, electrodes, and the recording instrument

Lead I = φLA − φRA
Lead II = φLL − φRA
Lead III = φLL − φLA
VWCT = (φRA + φLA + φLL) / 3

A chest lead measures its chest-electrode potential minus the Wilson central terminal. That average is a constructed reference, not a perfect physical zero. Adding the same offset C to both inputs cancels: (φ+ + C) − (φ− + C) = φ+ − φ−.

The instrument uses high input impedance and draws very little current. Ionic conduction in tissue meets electronic conduction through the electrode interface. A right-leg circuit commonly biases the body and reduces shared interference; it is separate from a lead’s subtraction rule. Real systems have finite rejection of shared noise and electrode artifacts. [5]

5. Recorded human action potentials

The fourth module includes original human LV optical mapping from Smirnov et al. (2020), shared under CC0. The 100 × 100 camera records at 1 kHz. The display retains 2,493 accepted sites in donor 1 and 455 in donor 2 after the disclosed quality mask. Each pixel averages fluorescence from tissue; it is not a single-cell electrode.

Four beats are aligned to the global pacing trigger, averaged, notch-filtered at 60 Hz and temporally smoothed. Sites are not individually time-aligned in the measured movie. The selected single-beat option uses the same processing without ensemble averaging. Amplitude is locally normalized fluorescence, not calibrated mV. Derived AT and RT₈₀ maps are estimates; sampling resolution is not timing accuracy. Processing and raw-file provenance ↗

6. A calibrated four-chamber source model

The population-average geometry is derived from 19 CT-based adult heart models. It retains the thick LV wall and prescribed source RV/atrial thicknesses. Its left atrial appendage was cropped in the original dataset; the labeled ostium is now connected to an inferred blind-ending pouch. The combined anatomy has 340,582 electrical activation nodes and 1,562,432 myocardial tetrahedra. The appendage’s shape is reconstructed, not measured. Rodero et al. ↗

The default ventricular recovery shape pools 2,948 accepted optical recording sites from two human donor preparations, giving each donor equal weight. Alignment and AP-duration normalization are used only to estimate the shape; the recorded movies remain unchanged. An assumed intrinsic upstroke replaces the broadened optical rise, and optical fluorescence does not calibrate absolute membrane mV. Atrial action potentials come from the published Courtemanche–Ramirez–Nattel ionic model. Local recovery remains AT + APD.

Vlead(t) = −∫ ∇Zlead · σi∇Vm(t) dΩ
Lead II = φLL − φRA

The reciprocal field Z is computed in a finite homogeneous ellipsoidal body with virtual boundary electrodes. The same spatial integral produces all twelve leads. The source field is refined to 2,400,926 voltage sites: activation and AP duration are interpolated to tetrahedral edge midpoints before the nonlinear AP is evaluated. This improves field sampling; it does not solve a finer activation graph or add biological measurements. A uniform membrane voltage still gives zero signal.

A calibrated median of 108 beats from a PTB healthy-control recording now acts as the lead-II fitting target. Several activation and cellular waveform alternatives were compared. Fifteen modeled ventricular delivery sites include basal RV coverage; activation timing, effective tissue source conductivities and regional AP durations are calibrated upstream. The finished ECG is calculated without inserting measured waveform samples or applying an ECG filter. Fitted conductivities are effective model parameters, not measured values from the anatomy donor.

The CT anatomy, optical donors and ECG recording belong to different people. A closer single-lead fit does not uniquely identify the real heart’s physiology; the other leads are not optimized, and most match this recording less closely. Graph activation, isotropic atrial propagation, a homogeneous body and the inferred LAA remain explicit approximations. Evidence for the recovery experiment

Higuchi & Nakaya (1984) changed epicardial temperature in seven dogs while recording endocardial and epicardial monophasic action potentials and a local electrogram. Changing the duration difference changed T-wave polarity. Boukens et al. (2015) recorded optical APs and pseudo-ECGs in ten human LV wedges and tested a three-dimensional ionic forward model. Their endpoint means support largely synchronized, mildly reversed recovery—not a universal reverse sequence across the human ventricle. The wave module’s human preset interpolates these summary values; it is not raw recorded AP data. Higuchi & Nakaya ↗ · Boukens et al. ↗

Why the wave signal depends on electrode geometry

Nearby electrodes weight an approaching source more strongly. The default strand now uses distant electrodes, while nearby electrodes and an imposed early-repolarization notch are optional experiments. The earlier 115 ms dip came from that assumed notch; a minimum-opacity current graphic exaggerated its appearance. The revised view shows the instantaneous phase, the spatial voltage range and the lead sensitivity. Quantitative diagnosis, assumptions & checks ↗
